# Day 5 — Consolidation {#sec-day5-consolidation}

**20 minutes · plenary**

## Say it in one sentence

Without notes, write the sentence you would say to a diabetes service that has
asked whether your model is any use. It must contain a metric, the number that
metric has to beat before it means anything, and the error type the service
actually cares about.

A sentence that meets the bar:

> On patients like these, the model ranks a diabetic patient above a
> non-diabetic one about four times in five, and at the default threshold it
> finds about half of the diabetic patients while predicting `neg` for
> everybody would be right 64% of the time — so the accuracy figure is not the
> one to judge it by.

Count how many of the three elements your own sentence has.

## Self-assessment

Tick honestly. Anything unticked is what to review before Day 6.

- [ ] I can define RMSE, MAE and R² and say which of the three changes most when five patients are badly predicted.
- [ ] I can explain why the same model can have R² 0.93 in one population and 0.2 in another.
- [ ] I quote the majority-class accuracy next to every accuracy I report.
- [ ] I can say what AUC is the probability of, in one sentence, without mentioning a threshold.
- [ ] I can produce a model with perfect training accuracy and explain why that is a warning rather than a result.
- [ ] I can say why hyperparameters are chosen on resampled training data and not on the test set.
- [ ] I can tell whether a difference between two models is larger than the noise in the comparison.

## Five questions

Answer in a sentence each. These are the form the written assessment takes.

1. A model predicting length of stay reports R² = 0.93 on one ward and R² =
   0.21 on another, with an MAE of about three and a half days on both. What
   has changed, and which of the two numbers would you put in the abstract?
2. A screening model reports 94% accuracy for a condition with 6% prevalence.
   Give the number you need next to it, and say what the model is probably
   doing.
3. Your decision tree has a training accuracy of 1.000. A colleague suggests
   collecting more data. Why will that not help, and what will?
4. You tune `tree_depth` by fitting twenty trees and keeping the one with the
   best test accuracy. Name what you have just lost, and what you should have
   resampled instead.
5. A random forest reaches a test AUC of 0.831 and a logistic regression 0.844
   on the same split, and the resampled standard error is 0.02. Write the
   sentence you would put in the results section.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Answers.** (1) The population changed, not the model: R² is a ratio whose
denominator is the variance of the outcome in the evaluation sample, and the
second ward's length of stay is less variable. The MAE in days is the number
for the abstract, with a baseline beside it. (2) The majority-class accuracy,
94%: the model is almost certainly predicting "negative" for everybody and
inheriting the prevalence. Ask for sensitivity. (3) More data does not reduce
capacity, and the tree will memorise the larger sample too; the cure is fewer
leaves — `tree_depth`, `min_n`, `cost_complexity` — chosen by resampling. (4)
You have lost the held-out estimate: the test set has been used twenty times to
make a choice, so its score is now an optimistic training score. Resample the
*training* rows, with `vfold_cv()` or `GridSearchCV(cv=...)`. (5) Something of
the form: "the two models performed indistinguishably (test AUC 0.83 and 0.84
against a resampled standard error of 0.02), so the simpler model is
preferred" — mark the word *indistinguishably* and the absence of the word
*better*.

**Rubric** (if the day is assessed, 20 marks):

| | Marks |
|---|---|
| Three regression metrics computed correctly on held-out rows, with a baseline | 4 |
| R² explained as depending on the evaluation population, not only the model | 3 |
| Classifier evaluated with sensitivity and specificity shown separately, and the majority-class accuracy quoted | 4 |
| A model with training accuracy 1.000 produced, and the test evidence that condemns it | 3 |
| Hyperparameters tuned by resampling the training rows, with the test set opened once | 4 |
| A model comparison stated with its uncertainty, not as a ranking | 2 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[80,20]"}

Mark the comparison, not the winner. A student whose forest beats the logistic
regression and who says so without a standard error has done less than one
whose forest loses and who explains why the loss is uninformative.
:::
:::

## What carries into Day 6

Three loose ends were left deliberately, and each opens the next session.

1. **The forest has no coefficients.** You tuned and evaluated a model you
   cannot describe to a clinician. @sec-importance, @sec-shap and @sec-dalex
   are about what can honestly be said about a model you cannot read.
2. **`mtry = 2` won, and nobody asked which two.** The forest's behaviour
   depends on which predictors it leans on, and nothing today measured that.
   Stretch 2 of @sec-random-forest — adding a column of random numbers and
   asking what importance it is given — is the direct hand-off.
3. **Every metric today was averaged over all patients.** MAE hides who is
   badly served and AUC hides it twice over. Subgroup performance is not on
   this module's timetable, so if you take one habit from today into your own
   work, take the habit of computing the metric again within each group you
   can define.
